To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) Twitter is not a good predictor of political popularity; (ii) the sentiment of tweet messages can be quantified using a statistical model with side information; (iii) tweet sentiment correlates well with the actual political sentiment in real world; and (iv) the sentiment of a tweet message can be quantified by its sentiment words and emoticons.

(a) Twitter activities are not necessarily a good indicator of the public opinion, (b) sentiment analysis is not a trivial task as it is often thought to be, and (c) the public opinion in social networks is correlated with the real world opinion

(1) the activities in Twitter does not necessarily reflect the public opinion towards a political party; (2) the sentiment analysis based on keyword matching or supervised classification with distant supervision does correlate with the actual sentiment in real world; (3) the statistical model for sentiment with side information such emoticons, hash tags and sentiment lexicon is able to predict the public opinion towards political parties.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following issues.
the quantification of public opinion in Twitter and the analysis of its relation with the actual election outcome.
the quantification of opinions in Twitter messages.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, while Twitter is an interesting platform for political discussion, it does not provide a reliable indicator of public opinion towards the political parties.
the UK election results were not reflected in the Twitter activities, and that the sentiment analysis results from Twitter were in fact consistent with the actual election result.
the public opinion at Twitter does not reflect the real world public opinion.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the sentiment in tweets does not reflect the actual public opinions in the real world.

we have quantified the public sentiment at the UK General Election 2010 using the Twitter data, and we have found that Twitter sentiment analysis is a promising way to understand the public opinions towards certain events.
the use of side information is important in sentiment detection, and the proposed statistical model is able to provide a better understanding of the public opinions towards political events.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of side information is crucial in sentiment analysis of tweet messages.
quantifying the public opinion in social media is possible but the results are only as good as the sentiment analysis model used.
it is important to quantify the strength of opinions in tweet messages so that the public opinion in online world can be mapped to the offline sentiment.
